references.text: Jesus declares himself Lord of the Sabbath – a direct parallel to Luke 6:5 in Matthew's account of the same event.
Mark's parallel account where Jesus says that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath, with the addition that the Sabbath was made for man's sake.
Jesus claims the authority of the Son of Man on earth to forgive sins, demonstrating his divine authority – the same authority he asserts over the Sabbath.
Jesus defends his activity on the Sabbath by pointing to the Father's constant work, thereby placing himself above the Sabbath commandment.
The original Sabbath commandment in the Ten Commandments, over which Jesus as the Son of Man claims lordship.
The Sabbath commandment repeated in Deuteronomy, where it is justified by deliverance from Egypt – the Sabbath was given for man's sake, supporting Jesus' claim to lordship over it.
The prophet Isaiah speaks of honoring the Sabbath and calling it a delight. Jesus as Lord of the Sabbath defines what it means to keep the Sabbath rightly.
Hosea is quoted by Jesus in the parallel account (Matt 12:7): "I desire mercy, not sacrifice" – the principle underlying Jesus' lordship over the Sabbath.
Daniel's vision of the Son of Man receiving power and dominion, the background for the title "Son of Man" that Jesus uses when declaring himself Lord of the Sabbath.
The immediate context where the disciples pick grain on the Sabbath and Jesus defends them by referring to David, leading up to the declaration in verse 5.
